newsitem.title: INDIA: Global firms keen on joint venture with India BGML.
newsitem.headline: Global firms keen on joint venture with India BGML.

text.p: Several foreign firms have offered to form joint ventures with state-run Bharat Gold Mines Ltd (BGML) to help revive the ailing firm, Mines Minister Birendra Prasad Baishya said on Tuesday.
"We have received many proposals," Baishya told a news conference. "Already many foreign companies are coming forward to work in BGML."

The Indian cabinet last month asked the government to seek a private joint venture partner for BGML. It had said that if a suitable partner was not found, BGML "may be allowed to be wound up under the provisions of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special provisions) Act".
BGML had been making losses for several years due to low ore recovery and was declared a sick company in 1992.
"Cost of production of 10 grammes of gold is 12,000 rupees which is 7,000 rupees higher than the market price," Baishya said.
The cabinet had decided that offers would be invited in an "open and transparent mode", and the search was likely to be completed in six months.
Baishya said that the government had formed a committee headed by B.B. Tandon, the highest-ranking civil servant in the Mines Ministry, to select the joint venture partner.
"We are examining the offers," Tandon said. He did not give the name of the companies which were keen on the joint venture.
Tandon said the equity participation in the joint venture would be decided after examining the offers.
Baishya said the government had options to either close down BGML, revive it with budgetary support or turn it around through a joint venture.

He said closing down the firm was against the interest of the BGML employees and the plan of reviving it through budgetary support was not viable as it would have required the fresh infusion of two billion rupees.
"Therefore the third option was most viable," Baishya said. "We are confident that we will be able to revive it with the help of a joint venture."
Tandon said foreign firms were interested in recovering gold from the 33 million tonnes of tailing dumps at BGML. Tailing dumps are the overburden left after gold is recovered.
Tandon estimated that about 24 tonnes of gold was present in the dumps out of which about 12 tonnes was recoverable.
